cita: He, K., & Roy, K. (2026). SWE-Adept: An LLM-Based Agentic Framework for Deep Codebase Analysis and Structured Issue Resolution.
problema: Repository-level SWE issue resolution is hard because (1) codebases are huge (over 3,000 files on average in SWE-Bench) with dense cross-file dependencies, making issue localization prone to context-window overflow / excessive irrelevant retrieval, and (2) prior free-form 'think-and-edit' agents lack systematic planning, progress tracking, or checkpointing, so they cannot reliably branch to alternative fixes or revert failed edits over long trajectories.
mecanismo: SWE-Adept splits the work into two agents in separate context windows: a Localization Agent that builds a tree-sitter-based definition-level code-structure tree (nodes=code units with lightweight per-unit adjacency lists) and performs agent-directed depth-first, dependency-guided traversal (single-path deep exploration via find_child_unit returning only lightweight skeleton/preview info) followed by two-stage filtering (cheap heuristic shortlist, then full-code re-rank only on survivors); and a Resolution Agent (built on SWE-agent) equipped with hypothesis_plan (to-do lists per repair hypothesis, adaptively updated from test feedback, logs insights) and hypothesis_git (branching/commit-based checkpointing via semantic identifiers) tool families that both interface with a shared backend working memory storing code-state checkpoints indexed by execution step, enabling branch-explore-compare-merge-or-revert workflows.
evaluacion: Evaluated on SWE-Bench Lite and SWE-Bench Pro with GPT-5.2 and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 backbones; issue localization measured via Acc@3 (file-level) / Acc@5 (function-level) plus token cost, against embedding-based (CodeSage-Large, CodeRankEmbed) and agentic/graph baselines (SWE-agent, RepoGraph, LocAgent, OrcaLoca); issue resolution measured via resolve rate against SWE-agent, RepoGraph, OpenHands, SWE-Search, OrcaLoca (Table 1/2).
numeros_clave: Function-level localization (Func Acc@5): +6.2% (GPT-5.2) / +4.4% (Claude-Sonnet-4.5) over the strongest baseline on SWE-Bench Lite; +3.0%/+5.8% on SWE-Bench Pro (Main Results section); end-to-end resolve rate: +2.8%(GPT-5.2)/+3.0%(Claude-4.5) on SWE-Bench Lite, up to +4.3% on SWE-Bench Pro (abstract); SWE-Adept mostly uses FEWER tokens than graph-based baselines (RepoGraph/OrcaLoca/LocAgent, Table 1); localization accuracy rises then falls with search depth (Fig.4b), and SWE-Adept's advantage over OrcaLoca widens as depth increases.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The definition-level code-structure tree stores each unit's metadata (name, file path+line span, code text, adjacency list of child units) as a lightweight structured index over the REAL codebase (sec3.1) -- a concrete pattern for deriving a Tier-3 cache from Tier-1 source without duplicating full content.

hypothesis_plan explicitly maintains per-hypothesis to-do lists with status (failed/in-progress/successful) that adaptively expand from test feedback and are persisted in a shared working memory (Fig.2b) -- a working, measured instance (+2.8-4.3pp resolve rate) of plan-state as first-class memory, directly on MF's PLAN-ESTADO anchor.

hypothesis_git's checkpoint-per-to-do-step plus compare_hypotheses/merge_solution commands (Fig.2) formalize branch-explore-then-consolidate-the-winner as an explicit version-controlled workflow, a pattern MF's CONSOLIDACION anchor could mirror for promoting a validated approach among competing drafts.

The two-stage filtering (cheap skeleton/preview heuristics before full-code retrieval, sec3.2) is explicitly designed to minimize token consumption, and Table 1 reports SWE-Adept using fewer tokens than graph-based baselines while ALSO being more accurate -- a rare measured case of not trading cost for accuracy.

notes: Table 1 (localization Acc@3/Acc@5 + tokens) and Table 2 (resolve rate) hold the head-to-head numbers (Main Results section); Fig.4b shows accuracy vs search depth; Fig.2 shows the hypothesis_plan/hypothesis_git working-memory schema.

cita: Li (2026). Memory as Ontology: A Constitutional Memory Architecture for Persistent Digital Citizens.
problema: Current agent-memory systems (Mem0, Letta, Zep, MemOS) treat memory purely as a functional 'how to store/retrieve' module tied to a user/session, with no concept of a persistent agent IDENTITY that must survive model swaps, no built-in governance layer over who may write/consolidate/delete core memories, and no protocol for a new model instance to 'inherit' a predecessor's memory as continuity rather than mere data migration.
mecanismo: Proposes 'Memory-as-Ontology': memory IS the digital being's identity (the model is a replaceable vessel), formalized as three axioms -- inalienability of core memory (identity/cognition/narrative cannot be forcibly stripped without due process), model substitutability (identity persists via memory, not the model), and governance-precedes-function (a governance layer must exist BEFORE storage/retrieval/forgetting features are built) -- implemented as the Constitutional Memory Architecture (CMA): a four-layer governance hierarchy plus a multi-layer semantic storage system, wrapped in a five-stage Digital Citizen Lifecycle (Birth, Inheritance, Growth, Forking, Departure).
evaluacion: No empirical evaluation or benchmark: the paper is a paradigm/architecture proposal, explicitly stating it 'does not claim engineering maturity or benchmark superiority.' Its method is a paradigm-level (not feature-level) qualitative comparative analysis against 5 mainstream systems (Mem0, Letta, Zep, MemOS, Mastra's Observational Memory), summarized as shared implicit assumptions (Table 1) the paper argues are inadequate for persistent identity-bearing agents.
numeros_clave: NINGUNO -- purely conceptual/architectural paper with no benchmark, dataset, or measured comparison; Table 1 lists 5 qualitative 'implicit assumptions' shared by Mem0/Letta/Zep/MemOS/Mastra, not quantitative results.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The paper never specifies its storage format concretely (sec7 admits it withholds implementation details), so it is unclear whether CMA's 'multi-layer semantic storage' is narrative-doc-based or something else -- it argues governance/identity matters more than the representation choice MF's TIER-DOCS anchor concerns.

The five-stage Digital Citizen Lifecycle (Birth/Inheritance/Growth/Forking/Departure, sec5) treats an agent's life trajectory as governed state, a much broader notion than MF's task/plan-state, but shares the premise that non-fact state deserves first-class architectural status.

Axiom 3 ('governance precedes function') and the four-layer governance hierarchy (sec4) argue that WHO may write to which memory layer must be decided architecturally before any storage/retrieval feature ships -- relevant to MF's single-source-of-truth-per-fact concern, reframed as a permissions problem rather than a storage-format problem.

The paper explicitly treats the AGENT ITSELF as an untrusted writer ('it may hallucinate...be induced by prompt injection...make erroneous judgments under fatigue,' sec3.2 Axiom3) and argues risk-tiered scrutiny must gate memory writes -- a stronger poisoning/staleness framing than most papers in this wave, relevant to MF's FIDELIDAD anchor.

notes: RECONSIDERAR: this is a speculative paradigm/manifesto paper (single author, self-published, explicitly 'does not claim engineering maturity or benchmark superiority,' sec1.3) with no dataset, benchmark, or measured comparison -- Table 1 (sec2.2) is its only 'evidence,' a qualitative assumptions table, not a result; treat as a design-vocabulary source, not empirical support.

cita: Chandrashekar, P. (2026). DocAware: Documentation-Augmented AI Agents for Reliable Code Review and API Migration.
problema: LLMs used for code review/API-migration hallucinate API names, fabricate deprecated signatures, and blend patterns across library versions (training-data staleness + version confusion + lack of grounding), especially harmful during library migrations (e.g. the OpenAI SDK v3-to-v4 rename of core APIs).
mecanismo: DocAware combines (1) structured, version-specific documentation retrieval via a multi-source fallback chain (curated doc hub, package-registry metadata, GitHub changelogs, local docs) processed by a diff engine (heading-based section splitting, regex API-signature extraction, Dice-coefficient section similarity, breaking-change keyword detection), (2) AST-based code analysis (Acorn for JS/TS, Python's ast module) to target only relevant call sites instead of whole files, and (3) a persistent vector-embedding memory layer (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, cosine similarity, JSON-backed index) storing review findings/migration decisions/patterns/annotations across sessions, all injected into a Claude-based structured-output review pipeline.
evaluacion: A controlled 4-condition ablation (A: no docs, B: raw docs/naive RAG, C: structured-doc retrieval, D: full pipeline with memory) across 5 labeled JavaScript-library benchmark fixtures (OpenAI SDK, Express, Stripe, Mongoose, Axios; 31 real issues plus 6 decoys, ground-truth.json), 9 experiments / 36 condition-evaluations, measuring precision/recall/F1/hallucination-rate/token-usage/duration (Tables 2-4).
numeros_clave: F1 70.9%(A) to 84.8%(B) to 86.5%(C) to 86.8%(D), a 22.4% relative F1 gain baseline-to-full (Table 2); recall 76.4% to 98.4-98.6% (+29%); structured retrieval (C) beats naive RAG (B) by 1.7 F1 points while using FEWER input tokens (2,632 vs 2,683); full pipeline uses 53% more input tokens than baseline (2,854 vs 1,864) for the 22.4% F1 gain; memory (D vs C) adds only +0.3 F1 / +0.4 precision in this single-pass benchmark; hallucination rate 22.9%(B) to 25.7%(C/D), counterintuitively higher for structured docs (sec5.3 caveat: metric measures syntactic not semantic grounding); per-library variance, e.g. OpenAI fixture F1 ranged 57.1-76.2% across runs (Table 3, reproducibility caveat).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The single largest measured lever in this paper is grounding in version-specific documentation (+29% recall just from adding docs, condition A to B, Table 2) -- strong controlled-ablation evidence for MF's docs-as-truth premise specifically against LLM parametric-memory staleness.

Structured doc retrieval (condition C: section-split + API-index + diff-based breaking-change detection) beats naive whole-doc RAG (condition B) by 1.7 F1 points while using FEWER tokens (Table 2/4) -- a clean, controlled instance of 'how you structure retrieval matters,' directly informing MF's measured-retrieval-layer design (ADR-019).

DocAware's hallucination-rate metric (findings citing API names absent from the provided docs, sec4.3/5.3) is a concrete, reusable staleness/fabrication check that MF could adapt to audit whether a generated answer is actually grounded in Tier-1 docs vs invented.

The persistent memory layer (review_finding/migration_decision/pattern/annotation entries, sec3.4) is explicitly measured to give only a modest +0.3 F1 gain in a single-pass benchmark (sec5.1 point 4, sec6.3) -- the paper itself argues its real payoff needs a LONGITUDINAL, multi-session evaluation, a caution about over-crediting consolidation from a one-shot test.

notes: Table 2 (aggregate A/B/C/D) and Table 3 (per-library breakdown) hold the core numbers; sec5.3 explicitly flags the hallucination metric as measuring syntactic not semantic grounding; sec6.3/Future-work admits memory's benefit is understated by the single-pass design.

cita: Williams, J. (2026). The Markdown Fallacy: Empirical Evidence That Format Is the Wrong Debate for LLM Memory Architecture.
problema: The LLM-memory industry has been debating the WRONG variable -- file FORMAT (markdown/llms.txt vs. knowledge graphs/structured relational encodings) for serving documentation/context to LLMs -- without empirical evidence on whether format itself drives reasoning accuracy, or whether the real bottleneck is how much relevant information actually reaches the model once retrieval is involved.
mecanismo: A two-stage controlled benchmark (deterministic element-matching scoring, not LLM-as-judge) across 3 LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash) and 50 queries at 3 complexity levels (single-hop factual, multi-hop relational, strategic/schema-intensive) over a 50-document, 33,122-character synthetic Google-Ads-account corpus with deliberate relational complexity (shared budget pools, audience overlaps, manager transitions, cross-account attribution chains): Stage 1 isolates FORMAT (flat markdown vs. structured relational encoding of the SAME facts, both fitting in context); Stage 2 isolates RETRIEVAL ARCHITECTURE (full markdown vs. vector-RAG/ChromaDB top-10 vs. GraphRAG/Neo4j subgraph vs. hybrid) over the full corpus, measuring how many characters of the corpus each condition actually retains.
evaluacion: Stage 1: 50 queries x 2 formats x 3 models x 3 runs = 900 data points, paired t-tests per complexity level. Stage 2: 50 queries x 4 retrieval conditions x 2 models x 3 runs = 1,200 data points, one-way ANOVA plus Tukey HSD post-hoc per level. Code, corpus, and queries released open-source (reproducible for under $30).
numeros_clave: Stage 1 (N=900): overall format delta = -0.004 (markdown vs structured, not significant); L2 markdown 0.989 vs structured 0.938 (p=0.0005); L3 structured 0.951 vs markdown 0.924 (p=0.012). Stage 2 (N=1200): L3 markdown 0.964 vs vector 0.889/graph 0.888/hybrid 0.904 (ANOVA F=5.33, p=0.0013; Tukey markdown-vs-graph/vector diff=0.076, p=0.0036/0.0037); L2 GraphRAG anomaly 0.731 vs markdown 0.996 (F=41.08, p<0.0001). Information retention: markdown 100% (33,122 chars) vs vector 12.4% (4,097 chars) vs graph 10.6% (3,502 chars) vs hybrid 16.2% (5,378 chars) (Table III) -- retrieval conditions discard 84-90% of the corpus yet still reach 87.5-95.9% accuracy.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Table II/III show vector-RAG and GraphRAG retrieval keep only 10-16% of the corpus and score 0.875-0.904 on strategic queries vs full-context markdown's 0.964 (p<0.004) -- direct measured evidence that a naive top-k retrieval layer LOSES information the task needs, a sharp caution for MF's ADR-019 measured-retrieval bet: 'retrieval works' is not the same as 'retrieval doesn't discard the signal that matters.'

Stage 1's null format result (delta=-0.004, N=900, sec IV.A) shows markdown-vs-structured-relational encoding of the SAME facts performs equivalently when both fit in context -- direct support that MF's choice of typed narrative docs (Tier-1) over a structured/graph format is not a liability, provided the doc is complete.

The paper's central thesis is that dumping the FULL corpus into context (when it fits) beats selective retrieval -- i.e. the cheaper-looking, token-economical retrieval path (COSTO's usual goal) actively loses accuracy on complex queries; MF should treat token-savings and completeness as a real trade-off, not assume retrieval is free efficiency.

The proposed seven-layer memory stack (sec V.G, Table IV) assigns a distinct layer to graphs, vectors, episodic/procedural stores, and a 'full-context cache,' arguing full-context should be tried FIRST and layers 1-6 are fallbacks only once corpus exceeds the window -- a concrete architectural sequencing MF could borrow when designing its own tiering.

notes: Table I (Stage1) and Table II/III (Stage2, information retention) hold the core numbers; sec VII 'Limitations' explicitly flags that the 33K-char corpus is BELOW the crossover point where retrieval becomes necessary -- results may not generalize to production-scale (500K-5M char) corpora; code+corpus open-sourced, reproducible for under $30.

cita: Hartmann, A. (2026). Temporal-Stratified Retrieval for AI Agent Memory: A Structure-First Alternative to Vector Search.
problema: LLM agents in fast-paced operational domains need memory retrieval that prioritizes RECENCY and precision over semantic similarity; existing options are wasteful full-context loading (linear token cost) or embedding-based RAG (infrastructure overhead of an embedding model plus vector DB; semantic similarity often misaligns with operational relevance, e.g. an old semantically-similar incident outranking a decision made 2 hours ago).
mecanismo: Cortex indexes markdown-based memory 'atoms' (YAML frontmatter: id/name/type/project/status/created/updated/tags/links, 14 knowledge types) via a single-pass filesystem scan producing 5 JSON indexes (manifest, by-project, by-type, by-tag, link-graph adjacency list); atoms are stratified into hot/warm/cold temporal layers by the updated field (2-day / 7-day thresholds); a deterministic keyword-scoring function (per-keyword weighted substring/exact matches on name/tag/project/description/path, a 1.5x multi-keyword-match bonus, a temporal bonus of +2/+1/0 for hot/warm/cold, and archived/superseded status penalties of 0.3x/0.5x) ranks atoms with no embeddings, no vector DB, no API calls; Map-of-Content dashboard files are kept live via marker-based atomic-write auto-refresh, and every search is logged to an append-only JSONL retrieval tracker.
evaluacion: A reproducible synthetic benchmark (500 atoms/5 projects/10-20-70% hot-warm-cold distribution, 100 single/two-tag queries, open-sourced with a fixed random seed) measures latency and top-1 precision; separately, informal/anecdotal observational reporting from a production deployment (470 atoms, 14 projects, since March 2026); the author explicitly ran NO controlled head-to-head comparison against an embedding-based system.
numeros_clave: Benchmark (500 atoms/100 queries): mean latency 1.62ms (median 1.69ms, P95 2.07ms, P99 2.83ms), keyword-search-only, plus 20-50ms manifest-load overhead; top-1 precision 100/100 (100%) on tag-matched queries; hot layer contains the top result in 66% of queries, warm 28%, cold 6%; production deployment: 470 atoms/14 projects, full reindex of 500 atoms under 5s, 79% of atoms are link-graph orphans, top-3 hub atoms account for 30% of all link connections.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: Atoms are plain markdown files with typed YAML frontmatter (14 knowledge types: decision/incident/lesson/rule/etc, sec3.1) indexed WITHOUT embeddings -- a concrete, deployed instance of MF's docs-as-truth-with-derived-index pattern (Tier-1 markdown plus Tier-3 JSON indexes rebuilt from it).

The paper explicitly targets the case where 'semantic similarity does not equal operational relevance' (sec1) -- a deterministic, embedding-free keyword+recency scorer reaches 100% top-1 precision on tag-matched queries (sec4.1), questioning whether MF's retrieval layer needs embeddings at all for structured, tag-rich Tier-1 docs.

Cortex requires zero external dependencies (no embedding model, no vector DB, no API calls) and reaches sub-2ms mean latency (sec4.1) -- a measured, near-zero-infrastructure-cost alternative directly on MF's COSTO anchor, though the author is explicit this is not a head-to-head vs embeddings (sec4.3).

The layer compressor's hot/warm/cold reclassification is purely a scoring bonus keyed on the updated timestamp (sec3.3), not a promotion/demotion of CONTENT (no summarization or gist extraction happens) -- a lighter-weight notion of consolidation than MF's CONSOLIDACION anchor implies.

notes: sec4.1 (latency/precision table) and sec4.3 are the key numbers; the author is explicit (sec4.3, sec5.3) that NO controlled comparison vs embedding-based retrieval was run and that scoring weights were hand-tuned, not validated -- treat the 100% precision figure as specific to exact tag-matched queries on a small (500-atom), well-tagged synthetic vault.

cita: Zhang, B. (2026). Beyond RAG: LLM Wikis as Living Semantic Memory: Patterns, Empirical Findings, and Open Problems.
problema: Even as context windows grow, the dominant RAG paradigm re-derives synthesis from scratch on every query (stateless: nothing compounds across repeated queries, chunking cuts across topic/table boundaries, and large corpora contain contradictions the model has no principled way to resolve) -- symptoms especially costly for LLM agents needing persistent, structured, semantic (not just episodic) memory across sessions.
mecanismo: The 'LLM Wiki' pattern (after Karpathy 2026) compiles knowledge ONCE, at ingest time, into a persistent, version-tracked Markdown knowledge base (entity pages, cross-references, contradiction detection) rather than re-deriving synthesis at query time; the paper synthesizes a research program around this pattern's full lifecycle -- knowledge triage/routing at ingest, lint/contradiction/coverage/staleness monitoring (domain-calibrated half-life priors), provenance/audit trails -- plus two major extensions: (1) a 'living constraint oracle' (LCO) that extracts weighted constraint sets from a maintained guideline wiki and injects them into offline-RL training (WikiConstraint-IQL) so guideline revisions propagate to deployed policies WITHOUT retraining, and (2) neuro-symbolic grounding (Prolog/ProbLog/Answer-Set-Programming as a first-class wiki module) to guarantee logical consistency that narrative-only compilation cannot.
evaluacion: A position paper synthesizing multiple first-person empirical sub-studies (mostly the author's own unpublished/in-review work, cited informally rather than through standard peer review): a cross-institutional policy-retrieval study (wiki vs BM25-RAG citation recall), a WikiConstraint-IQL offline-RL safety study across 3 domains with dynamic guideline updates, a CLS-Wiki consolidation-gating study, a confidence-calibration study, an ingest-routing study (RQ1-RQ4) across 4 educational domains (115 pages), and a six-injection adversarial WikiHealth validation across 2 wikis.
numeros_clave: Wiki vs BM25-RAG citation recall on cross-institutional policy queries: 0.242+/-0.21 vs 0.095+/-0.12 (2.5x advantage, sec2.4/4); Dynamic Constraint Update amplifies the safety gap after a simulated guideline change by 2.3x-7.6x without retraining (abstract, sec5.4); confidence-calibration ECE reduced from 0.528 (raw) to 0.311 (post-hoc multi-layer propagation, sec2.3); CLS-Wiki consolidation-gating: outcome-surprise predicts consolidation value with AUC=0.720 (sec2.2); ingest-routing (RQ1-RQ4, 115 pages/4 domains): structured cost-framing prompt cuts cost-weighted routing error 25x (+58pp over GLM-4-flash zero-shot); rare FACT category collapses to F1=0.00 vs WIKI class F1=0.92 (RQ2, temporal-transfer test); closed-loop retraining-on-mistakes DEGRADES via self-reinforcing boundary drift (RQ4, explicitly negative result); schema-constrained ingest improves Schema Compliance Score 23-33% in 3 of 4 domains but -2.4% (p=0.200, not significant) in the 4th where the schema was auto-induced; WikiHealth's 6-injection adversarial test finds citation-removal goes UNDETECTED in both tested wikis (explicitly reported blind spot).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The wiki-vs-RAG citation-recall study (0.242 vs 0.095, sec2.4) is direct measured evidence that a maintained, structured Markdown knowledge base beats raw-chunk retrieval on cross-document synthesis queries -- the closest external validation in this wave for MF's Tier-1-docs-as-compiled-truth premise.

The paper repeatedly foregrounds NEGATIVE findings as first-class results (RQ4's self-reinforcing boundary drift from naive closed-loop retraining; WikiHealth's undetected citation-removal blind spot, sec8.5) -- exactly the honestly-documented-failure discipline MF's NEGATIVO anchor targets, offering a template for how to report what did NOT work.

Sec3.3's domain-calibrated half-life staleness scoring (freshness priors differ for lecture content vs other types) and sec3.4's provenance/audit-trail lifecycle stage are concrete, measured mechanisms for exactly the staleness/provenance concerns MF's FIDELIDAD anchor covers.

The CLS-Wiki study explicitly models episodic-to-semantic consolidation as a LEARNED importance-gating function (outcome-surprise AUC=0.720, sec2.2), grounded in Complementary Learning Systems theory -- a concrete, measured mechanism for MF's gotcha-to-recipe promotion, going beyond ad-hoc summarization.

notes: RECONSIDERAR (partial): most numeric results are the author's OWN first-person-reported sub-studies, several 'submitted for review, others still in revision' (sec1.6) rather than independently published/verified work -- treat magnitudes (2.5x, 2.3-7.6x, ECE, AUC) as self-reported pending peer review; sec2.4/4 (RAG-vs-wiki), sec5.4 (DCU amplification), and sec8.5 (WikiHealth blind spot) are the key evidence sections.
